plugin.endian.title: Byte order: big-endian and little-endian
plugin.endian.preset.aes-word: AES key word w0 = 0x2B7E1516 (FIPS 197): the key bytes are big-endian, a u32 on x86 is little-endian
plugin.endian.param.valueHint: Write the number as usual, e.g. 0x0A0B0C0D; shorter values are padded with leading zeros.
plugin.endian.param.widthHint: How many bytes the integer occupies in memory.
plugin.endian.region.value: Value as written (most significant byte first)
plugin.endian.step.initial: The {{bits}}-bit integer 0x{{value}} is about to be stored in memory twice: once big-endian, once little-endian. Both memory rows are still empty. Step forward to see how the bytes are placed.
plugin.endian.step.split: 0x{{value}} is a {{bits}}-bit integer, so it needs {{count}} bytes. Written down, the most significant byte (MSB) {{msb}} comes first and the least significant byte (LSB) {{lsb}} last. Memory has no "left" or "right", only addresses – so which byte goes to the lowest address?
plugin.endian.step.storeBigFirst: Big-endian: the big end comes first. Address +{{address}} gets the most significant byte {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}).
plugin.endian.step.storeBigMiddle: Big-endian: address +{{address}} gets the next byte in written order, {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}).
plugin.endian.step.storeBigLast: Big-endian: the highest address +{{address}} gets the least significant byte {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}). Memory now reads exactly like the written number.
plugin.endian.step.storeLittleFirst: Little-endian: the little end comes first. Address +{{address}} gets the least significant byte {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}).
plugin.endian.step.storeLittleMiddle: Little-endian: address +{{address}} gets the next more significant byte, {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}).
plugin.endian.step.storeLittleLast: Little-endian: the highest address +{{address}} gets the most significant byte {{byte}} (bits {{high}}–{{low}}). Memory now holds the written number in reverse byte order.
plugin.endian.step.compare: Same number, two layouts: big-endian {{big}} with the MSB {{msb}} at +0, little-endian {{little}} with the LSB {{lsb}} at +0. Network protocols use big-endian, and AES key bytes read as 32-bit words match big-endian; x86 and most ARM CPUs store integers little-endian, so code that loads key bytes as a native u32 must swap them.
plugin.endian.error.invalidParams: Give the value as hex text and pick a width.
plugin.endian.error.empty: Enter at least one byte of hex.
plugin.endian.error.width: Unknown width "{{width}}"; choose u16, u32 or u64.
plugin.endian.error.tooWide: The value needs {{length}} bytes but a {{width}} has only {{bytes}}.
